topic: understanding the concept of exponential decay and half-life applications

easy.text: Exponential decay describes a quantity that:

options.text: Decreases by a consistent PERCENTAGE (proportional amount) over equal time periods
options.feedback: Correct -- exponential decay involves multiplying by the same fractional/percentage reduction factor repeatedly, unlike linear decay's fixed subtraction amount.

options.text: Decreases by the exact same fixed NUMBER each time period
options.feedback: That describes LINEAR decay, not exponential decay, which specifically involves a consistent PERCENTAGE reduction, not a fixed numerical subtraction.
This describes exponential GROWTH, essentially the opposite of exponential DECAY, which specifically describes a quantity DECREASING over time.

options.text: Remains exactly constant, with absolutely no change over time
options.feedback: This describes a constant/unchanging quantity, not exponential decay, which specifically involves ongoing, consistent proportional DECREASE.

medium.text: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 20 years, starting with 320 grams. How much will remain after 60 years?

options.feedback: This is the amount remaining after only 2 half-lives (40 years), not after 3 half-lives (60 years).
This is the amount remaining after only 1 half-life (20 years), not after 3 half-lives (60 years).
Exponential decay approaches but never mathematically reaches exactly zero after a finite number of half-lives -- there's always some remaining amount, however small.

hard.text: A medication's concentration in the bloodstream decreases exponentially, with a 'biological half-life' of 4 hours. If a patient needs the concentration to drop below 6.25% of the original dose before it's safe to take another dose, approximately how many hours must they wait? (Hint: figure out how many half-lives are needed to reach 6.25%)

options.feedback: Correct -- 6.25% equals 1/16 of the original amount, and since each half-life halves the amount (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16), reaching 1/16 requires 4 half-lives: 4×4 hours=16 hours.
This is just ONE half-life, which would only reduce the concentration to 50%, far more than the required 6.25% threshold.
This is only 2 half-lives, reducing concentration to 25%, which is still more than the required 6.25% threshold.
This incorrectly treats the 6.25% value directly as a time value, rather than correctly determining how many half-life PERIODS are needed to reach that percentage.

easy.hard: This decline pattern involves a consistent proportional reduction factor applied repeatedly across successive equal time intervals.
easy.medium: This is when something shrinks by the same percentage each time period, not the same fixed amount.
easy.easy: This is when something shrinks by the same percentage each time, not the same fixed amount.

medium.hard: Determine the number of complete half-life intervals within the elapsed time, then apply that many successive halving operations to the starting quantity.
medium.medium: Figure out how many 20-year periods fit into 60 years, then cut the starting amount in half that many times.

hard.hard: Express the target percentage as a power of one-half, then determine the corresponding number of half-life periods and convert to actual elapsed time.
hard.medium: Figure out how many times you need to cut something in half to get down to 6.25% (that's 1/16), then multiply that count by the 4-hour half-life.
hard.easy: 1/16 requires cutting in half 4 times, and 4 half-lives × 4 hours = 16 hours.
